Field surveys of Goldband goatfish (Upeneus moluccensis) in the coastal waters of the South China Sea have provided detailed morphometric data from photographic records of captured specimens. By measuring total length (TL) and applying a conversion factor of 0.9 to derive fork length from total length, researchers estimated that the ultimate fork length attainable by this species is 19.8 centimeters [Li = 19.8 centimeters]. This value represents the maximum fork length observed among mature individuals in the sampled population, marking the upper boundary of somatic growth under prevailing environmental conditions. The conversion from total length to fork length is a standard practice in fisheries biology, as fork length offers a more stable and reliable metric for comparative growth studies, particularly for species with slightly damaged or worn caudal fins. The relationship FL equals 0.9 times TL was derived empirically from a subset of undamaged specimens and proved consistent across the size range examined. This ultimate size is comparable to values reported for other congeneric goatfishes inhabiting similar demersal habitats, suggesting a conserved growth trajectory within the genus.

Reproductive biology studies conducted on Upeneus moluccensis have established that the onset of gonadal maturation occurs at a fork length of 12.6 centimeters [Lp = 12.6 centimeters]. Individuals below this size threshold are typically immature, with inactive gonads and no evidence of recent or imminent spawning activity. The size at puberty is a critical life-history parameter because it defines the transition from the juvenile phase to the reproductively viable portion of the population. In the sampled aggregation, the smallest individual with fully developed gonads or evidence of prior spawning measured 12.6 centimeters fork length, and this value has been adopted as the benchmark for length at maturity in regional stock assessments. This reproductive milestone appears to be reached within the first year of life for most individuals under the warm thermal regime characteristic of tropical inshore environments. The attainment of puberty at a relatively modest size compared to the ultimate fork length suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive output, an adaptation common among short-lived, fast-growing teleosts subject to high natural mortality rates.

The maximum reproductive rate of female Goldband goatfish was estimated from intensive field sampling conducted during the peak spawning season at a water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, gravid females were observed to produce an average of 62,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 62,000 eggs per spawning event] and to spawn approximately once daily during the spawning window [F_R_i = approximately once daily during the spawning window]. This extraordinarily high fecundity, combined with daily spawning frequency, underscores the species' capacity for rapid population turnover in favorable environments. The daily reproductive output of 62,000 eggs per day is among the highest recorded for mullid fishes of comparable body size, reflecting a reproductive strategy that maximizes propagule output over a relatively brief reproductive lifespan. The association between elevated water temperatures and peak spawning activity is well documented in tropical marine fishes, and the consistent temperature of 27.2 °C recorded during the sampling period indicates that this species spawns optimally within a narrow thermal range characteristic of its shallow-water, sandy-bottom habitat.

Neonatal life begins with the emergence of a yolk-sac larva from a pelagic egg measuring approximately 1 millimeter in diameter. Based on the egg diameter, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.00062 grams [Wwb = 0.00062 grams], derived from the spherical volume formula assuming a density approximating that of seawater. This minuscule initial mass reflects the enormous fecundity of the species, as energy is partitioned into a prodigious number of small, planktonic offspring rather than a few large, well-provisioned ones. The yolk-sac larva is entirely lecithotrophic during the first few days post-hatching, relying on endogenous yolk reserves while the mouth, gut, and sensory apparatus undergo critical development. The transition to exogenous feeding coincides with yolk absorption completion and swim bladder inflation, marking a vulnerable period of high mortality during which the tiny larvae must encounter suitable prey items at sufficient densities. The relationship between egg size and larval survival is a central theme in fish early life-history ecology, and the small egg size of Upeneus moluccensis indicates a reliance on high fecundity and good environmental timing rather than large per-offspring investment.

Longevity estimates for the Goldband goatfish derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith increment analysis conducted at a consistent water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] indicate a maximum lifespan of 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days]. This lifespan, equivalent to approximately five years, is relatively short for a demersal fish of this family, though consistent with the species' fast growth and early maturation schedule observed in tropical environments. The thermal regime at 27.2 °C appears to accelerate metabolic and developmental rates, compressing the life cycle into a narrower temporal window compared to populations inhabiting cooler subtropical waters. Annual mortality rates are correspondingly high, with few individuals surviving beyond the third year in heavily fished areas. Nonetheless, the combination of early puberty, prodigious daily fecundity, and a moderate lifespan ensures that even a single female surviving to reproductive age can contribute substantially to the next generation. The maximum observed age of 1,825 days serves as an important input parameter for demographic models used to evaluate sustainable harvest levels and population resilience under varying fishing pressures.
